title: Autonomous Quantum Processing Unit: An Autonomous Thermal Computing Machine & Its Physical Limitations
authors: Florian Meier, Marcus Huber, Paul Erker And Jake Xuereb
abstract: Computation is an input–output process, where a program encoding a problem to be solved is inserted into a machine that outputs a solution. Quantum computation conventionally relies on classical, external control outside the quantum computer to execute a program, obscuring computational and thermodynamic resources required. To understand the fundamental limits of computation, however, it is pivotal to work with a fully self-contained description of a quantum computation modeling the resources on the same footing as the computation itself. By developing a framework that we dub the autonomous Quantum Processing Unit (aQPU) we model quantum computation in the framework of autonomous thermal machines. Consisting of an internal quantum timekeeping mechanism, instruction register and memory system the aQPU allows investigating relationships between thermodynamic cost, complexity, speed and fidelity of a desired quantum computation.
tldr: The paper introduces an autonomous Quantum Processing Unit (aQPU) modeled as a thermal machine, analyzing the thermodynamic costs and physical limitations of quantum computation.
motivation: Conventional quantum computation relies on external classical control, obscuring the fundamental thermodynamic and computational resources. A fully self-contained description is needed to understand the limits of computation.
method: The authors develop a framework for an autonomous Quantum Processing Unit (aQPU) that includes an internal quantum clock, instruction register, and memory, treating quantum computation as an autonomous thermal machine.
result: The framework allows investigation of relationships between thermodynamic cost, complexity, speed, and fidelity of quantum computations, revealing physical limitations.
conclusion: Modeling quantum computation as an autonomous thermal machine provides insights into the fundamental resources required, bridging quantum thermodynamics and computation.

title: A Complete Theory Of The Clifford Commutant
authors: Lennart Bittel, Jens Eisert, Lorenzo Leone, Antonio A. Mele, And Salvatore F.E. Oliviero
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2171 (2026).

The Clifford group plays a central role in quantum information science. It is the building block for many error-correcting schemes and matches the first three moments of the Haar measure over the unitary group-a property that is essential for a broad range of quantum algorithms, with applications in pseudorandomness, learning theory, benchmarking, and entanglement distillation. At the heart of understanding many properties of the Clifford group lies the Clifford commutant: the set of operators that commute with [MATH]-fold tensor powers of Clifford unitaries. Previous understanding of this commutant has been limited to relatively small values of [MATH], constrained by the number of qubits [MATH]. In this work, we develop a complete theory of the Clifford commutant. Our first result provides an explicit orthogonal basis for the commutant and computes its dimension for arbitrary [MATH] and [MATH]. We also introduce an alternative and easy-to-manipulate basis formed by isotropic sums of Pauli operators. We show that this basis is generated by products of permutations, which generate the unitary group commutant, and at most three other operators. Additionally, we develop a graphical calculus allowing a diagrammatic manipulation of elements of this basis. These results enable a wealth of applications: among others, we characterize all measurable magic measures and identify optimal strategies for stabilizer property testing, whose success probability also offers an operational interpretation to stabilizer entropies. Finally, we show that these results also generalize to multi-qudit systems with prime local dimension.

.
tldr: This paper develops a complete theory of the Clifford commutant, providing an explicit orthogonal basis and dimension for arbitrary numbers of copies and qubits, with applications to magic measures and stabilizer property testing.
motivation: The Clifford group is central to quantum information, but the structure of its commutant was only known for limited cases. Understanding the commutant is key to characterizing magic, stabilizer testing, and other applications.
method: The authors derive an explicit orthogonal basis for the Clifford commutant and compute its dimension for arbitrary t and n. They introduce an alternative basis formed by isotropic sums of Pauli operators, generated by permutations and at most three other operators, and develop a graphical calculus.
result: They characterize all measurable magic measures, identify optimal strategies for stabilizer property testing, and show that stabilizer entropies have an operational interpretation as success probabilities. The results generalize to multi-qudit systems with prime local dimension.
conclusion: The complete theory of the Clifford commutant enables a wealth of applications in quantum information, including magic state resource theory and property testing, and provides a powerful tool for analyzing the Clifford group.

title: Geometric Speed Limit Of State Preparation And Curved Control Spaces
authors: Maximilian Goll And Robert H. Jonsson
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2160 (2026).

The preparation of quantum many-body systems faces the difficulty that in a realistic scenario only few control parameters of the system may be accessible. In this context, an interesting connection between the energy fluctuations during state preparation and its geometric length as measured by the Fubini-Study metric was discussed by Bukov et al. in 2019 [5]. An inspiring conjecture lower bounding the energy fluctuations by the minimal geometric length of all accessible state preparation protocols was put forward together with supporting examples and numerical evidence. However, we here show that the conjecture does not hold but can be violated if the accessible parameter space has extrinsic curvature, when embedded into the space of all dynamically accessible states. We illustrate this by a number of generic qubit, qutrit and harmonic oscillator systems.

.
tldr: This paper disproves a conjecture linking energy fluctuations to geometric length in state preparation, showing that curved control spaces can violate the bound.
motivation: Understanding fundamental limits on state preparation is crucial for quantum control; a geometric bound on energy fluctuations would have broad implications.
method: The authors analyze the geometry of control parameter spaces and the Fubini-Study metric, constructing counterexamples in qubit, qutrit, and harmonic oscillator systems.
result: They demonstrate that the conjectured lower bound fails when the accessible parameter space has extrinsic curvature, and provide explicit violations.
conclusion: The geometric speed limit is not universal; curvature of the control space must be accounted for in fundamental limits on state preparation.

title: From Superradiance To Superabsorption: An Exact Treatment Of Non-Markovian Cooperative Radiation
authors: Ignacio González And Ángel Rivas
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2159 (2026).

We investigate the emergence of cooperative radiation phenomena in ensembles of two-level atoms coupled to a lossy resonant cavity beyond the Markovian and mean-field approximations. By deriving a complete analytical solution for the two-emitter case and employing a numerically exact method for larger ensembles, we characterize the full transition from Markovian to non-Markovian collective dynamics for systems of up to [MATH] emitters. Our results reveal three distinct regimes: a Markovian phase exhibiting the standard superradiant burst, a non-Markovian phase featuring spontaneous superabsorption of the emitted field, and a critical regime marked by pulsed collective emission. We show that the critical spectral width separating these behaviors increases monotonically with the number of emitters, demonstrating that environmental memory effects can be enhanced by cooperativity. Finally, we find that the superradiant scaling of the peak intensity progressively degrades with increasing system size, approaching a subquadratic law in the limit of a perfect cavity. In this regime, spontaneous superabsorption emerges as a distinct manifestation of non-Markovian cooperativity.

.
tldr: This paper provides an exact analytical and numerical treatment of non-Markovian cooperative radiation in ensembles of two-level atoms coupled to a lossy cavity, revealing regimes of superradiance and superabsorption.
motivation: Understanding cooperative radiation beyond Markovian and mean-field approximations is crucial for quantum technologies, as environmental memory effects can significantly alter collective dynamics.
method: The authors derive a complete analytical solution for two emitters and use a numerically exact method for larger ensembles, solving the full non-Markovian dynamics without approximations.
result: Three distinct regimes are identified: Markovian superradiance, non-Markovian superabsorption, and a critical regime with pulsed emission. The critical spectral width increases with emitter number, and superradiant peak intensity degrades to subquadratic scaling in the perfect cavity limit.
conclusion: Non-Markovian cooperativity can enhance environmental memory effects and lead to spontaneous superabsorption, which is a distinct manifestation of collective dynamics beyond standard superradiance.

title: Towards Unconditional Uncloneable Encryption
authors: Pierre Botteron, Anne Broadbent, Eric Culf, Ion Nechita, Clément Pellegrini, And Denis Rochette
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2157 (2026).

Uncloneable encryption is a cryptographic primitive which encrypts a classical message into a quantum ciphertext, such that two quantum adversaries are limited in their capacity of being able to simultaneously decrypt, given the key and quantum side-information produced from the ciphertext. Since its initial proposal and scheme in the random oracle model by Broadbent and Lord [TQC 2020], uncloneable encryption has developed into an important primitive at the foundation of quantum uncloneability for cryptographic primitives. Despite sustained efforts, however, the question of unconditional uncloneable encryption (and in particular of the simplest case, called an uncloneable bit) has remained elusive. Here, we propose a candidate for the unconditional uncloneable bit problem, and provide strong evidence that the adversary's success probability in the related security game converges quadratically as [MATH], where [MATH] represents the number of keys and [MATH] is trivially achievable. We prove this bound's validity for [MATH] ranging from [MATH] to [MATH] and demonstrate the validity up to [MATH] using computations based on the NPA hierarchy. We furthemore provide compelling heuristic evidence towards the general case. In addition, we prove an asymptotic upper bound of [MATH] and give a numerical upper bound of [MATH], which to our knowledge is the best-known value in the unconditional model.

.
tldr: Proposes a candidate for unconditional uncloneable encryption and provides strong evidence for its security.
motivation: Uncloneable encryption is a fundamental primitive in quantum cryptography, but unconditional security (without random oracles) has remained elusive.
method: The authors propose a scheme for uncloneable bit encryption and analyze its security using the NPA hierarchy and heuristic arguments.
result: They prove a quadratic bound on the adversary's success probability for up to 5 keys and provide numerical evidence for up to 10 keys, with an asymptotic upper bound of 0.75.
conclusion: The work provides strong evidence that unconditional uncloneable encryption is achievable, advancing the foundations of quantum cryptography.

title: A Complexity Theory For Non-local Quantum Computation
authors: Andreas Bluhm, Simon Höfer, Alex May, Mikka Stasiuk, Philip Verduyn Lunel, And Henry Yuen
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2152 (2026).

Non-local quantum computation (NLQC) replaces a local interaction between two systems with a single round of communication and shared entanglement. Despite many partial results, it is known that a characterization of entanglement cost in at least certain NLQC tasks would imply significant breakthroughs in complexity theory. Here, we avoid these obstructions and take an indirect approach to understanding resource requirements in NLQC, which mimics the approach used by complexity theorists: we study the relative hardness of different NLQC tasks by identifying resource efficient reductions between them. Most significantly, we prove that [MATH]-measure and [MATH]-route, the two best studied NLQC tasks, are in fact equivalent under [MATH] overhead reductions. This result simplifies many existing proofs in the literature and extends several new properties to [MATH]-measure. For instance, we obtain sub-exponential upper bounds on [MATH]-measure for all functions, and efficient protocols for functions in the complexity class [MATH]. Beyond this, we study a number of other examples of NLQC tasks and their relationships.

.
tldr: This paper develops a complexity-theoretic framework for non-local quantum computation, showing equivalence between key tasks and establishing resource-efficient reductions.
motivation: Characterizing the entanglement cost of non-local quantum computation (NLQC) is known to be hard; the authors aim to circumvent this by studying relative hardness via reductions, similar to complexity theory.
method: The authors define resource-efficient reductions between NLQC tasks and prove that the two main tasks, f-measure and f-route, are equivalent under sub-exponential overhead reductions.
result: They obtain sub-exponential upper bounds on f-measure for all functions and efficient protocols for functions in the complexity class P, simplifying many existing proofs.
conclusion: The equivalence result extends properties between NLQC tasks and provides a complexity-theoretic lens for understanding non-local quantum computation.

title: Entanglement In The Dicke Subspace
authors: Aabhas Gulati, Ion Nechita, And Clément Pellegrini
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2150 (2026).

We provide a complete mathematical theory for the entanglement of mixtures of Dicke states. These quantum states form an important subclass of bosonic states arising in the study of indistinguishable particles. We introduce a tensor-based parametrization where the diagonal entries of these states are encoded as a symmetric tensor, enabling a direct translation between entanglement properties and well-studied convex cones of tensors. Our results bridge multipartite entanglement theory with semialgebraic geometry and the theory of completely positive and copositive tensors. This dictionary maps separability to completely positive tensors, the PPT property to moment tensors, entanglement witnesses to copositive tensors, and decomposable witnesses to sum of squares tensors. We establish that PPT entanglement exists for all multipartite systems with local dimension [MATH] and [MATH] parties, disproving a recent conjecture. We also show that, for mixtures of Dicke states, the PPT condition with respect to the most balanced bipartition implies all other PPT conditions. We further connect bosonic extendibility of mixtures of Dicke states to the duals of known hierarchies for non-negative polynomials, such as the ones by Reznick and Polya. We thus provide semidefinite programming relaxations for separability and entanglement testing in the Dicke subspace.

.
tldr: Provides a complete mathematical theory for entanglement of mixtures of Dicke states using tensor-based parametrization and convex cone theory.
motivation: To understand entanglement in bosonic systems of indistinguishable particles, which is important for multipartite quantum information.
method: Introduces a tensor parametrization mapping separability to completely positive tensors, PPT to moment tensors, and entanglement witnesses to copositive tensors; uses semialgebraic geometry and semidefinite programming relaxations.
result: Proves existence of PPT entanglement for all multipartite systems with local dimension ≥2 and ≥3 parties, disproving a recent conjecture; shows PPT condition for most balanced bipartition implies all others.
conclusion: Establishes a rich connection between entanglement theory and tensor cones, providing new tools for entanglement detection in Dicke subspace.

title: Measuring Rényi Entropy With An Echo Protocol
authors: Yi-Neng Zhou, Robin Löwenberg, And Julian Sonner
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2146 (2026).

We present efficient and practical protocols to measure the second Rényi entropy, whose exponential is known as the purity. Our approach is based on expressing the purity in terms of transition probabilities generated by an echo-type forward-backward evolution sequence, making it applicable to quantum many-body systems. Notably, our approach does not rely on random-noise averaging, a feature that can be extended to protocols to measure out-of-time-order correlation functions, as we demonstrate. By way of example, we show that our protocols can be practically implemented in superconducting qubit-based platforms, as well as in cavity-QED trapped ultra-cold gases.

.
tldr: Presents efficient echo-based protocols to measure the second Rényi entropy (purity) in quantum many-body systems without random-noise averaging.
motivation: Measuring Rényi entropy is crucial for characterizing entanglement and quantum correlations, but existing methods often require random averaging or are inefficient.
method: The purity is expressed in terms of transition probabilities from an echo-type forward-backward evolution sequence, avoiding random-noise averaging; the protocol is extended to out-of-time-order correlators.
result: The protocols are shown to be practically implementable on superconducting qubit platforms and in cavity-QED trapped ultracold gases.
conclusion: The work provides a practical, noise-robust method for measuring Rényi entropy, advancing experimental quantum information processing.

title: Thermodynamic Costs And Finite-power Efficiency Of Dephasing-assisted Quantum Heat Engines
authors: Susana F Huelga And Martin B Plenio Raphael Weber
abstract: Quantum heat engines (QHEs) are commonly believed to achieve their optimal efficiency only when operated quasi-statically. When running at finite power, however, they suffer effective friction due to the generation of coherences and transitions between energy eigenstates. It was noted that it is possible to increase the power of a QHE using external control schemes or suitable dephasing noise. Here, we investigate the thermodynamic cost associated with dephasing noise schemes using both numerical and analytical methods. Our findings unveil that the observed gain in power is generally not free of thermodynamic costs, as it involves energy costs of the control fields or heat flows between thermal and dephasing baths. These contributions must be duly accounted for when determining the engine’s overall efficiency. We identify suitable regimes in which, at a fixed effective dephasing rate, the heat leaked into the explicitly modelled dephasing bath can be made arbitrarily small, so that the efficiency at finite power approaches that of a quasi-statically operated Otto engine even when the dephasing environment is fully accounted for.
tldr: This paper investigates the thermodynamic costs of dephasing noise in quantum heat engines, showing that the power gain from dephasing comes at a cost, but can be made negligible in certain regimes.
motivation: Quantum heat engines suffer friction at finite power due to coherences; dephasing noise can increase power, but its thermodynamic cost was unclear.
method: The authors use numerical and analytical methods to model a quantum Otto engine with a dephasing bath, accounting for energy costs of control fields and heat flows.
result: They find that the power gain from dephasing involves energy costs, but in certain regimes the heat leaked into the dephasing bath can be made arbitrarily small.
conclusion: The efficiency at finite power can approach that of a quasi-static Otto engine even when the dephasing environment is fully accounted for, provided the dephasing rate is chosen appropriately.

title: Gap Between Quantum Theory Based On Real And Complex Numbers Is Arbitrarily Large
authors: Shubhayan Sarkar, David Trillo, Marc Olivier Renou And Remigiusz Augusiak
abstract: Quantum information theory, the formalism for representing information contained in quantum systems, is based on complex Hilbert spaces. It was recently shown that in quantum networks involving three parties with nontrivial locality constraints, this formalism predicts correlations that cannot be explained by real quantum theory, a variant of quantum mechanics based on real Hilbert spaces. In this work, we study a scenario with parties sharing quantum systems in a star network. We then construct a multipartite Bell inequality that exhibits a gap between quantum theory and its variant based on real numbers, which grows linearly with , and is thus arbitrarily large in the asymptotic limit. This implies, that, as the number of parties grows, Hilbert space formalism based on real numbers becomes exceedingly worse at describing complex networks of quantum systems. We also compute the tolerance of this gap to experimental errors.
tldr: This paper shows that the gap between real and complex quantum theory in star networks grows linearly with the number of parties, making real quantum theory arbitrarily worse for describing quantum networks.
motivation: Recent work demonstrated that complex Hilbert spaces are necessary to explain correlations in certain quantum networks. This paper aims to quantify how much worse real quantum theory becomes as the network size increases.
method: The authors construct a multipartite Bell inequality for a star network and analyze the violation achievable by complex versus real quantum theory, deriving a linear scaling of the gap with the number of parties.
result: The gap between the maximal violation in complex quantum theory and that in real quantum theory grows linearly with the number of parties, becoming arbitrarily large in the asymptotic limit. The tolerance to experimental errors is also computed.
conclusion: Real quantum theory becomes increasingly inadequate for describing quantum networks as the number of parties grows, highlighting the fundamental role of complex numbers in quantum information.

title: Non-commutative Optimization Problems With Differential Constraints
authors: Mateus Araújo, Andrew J. P. Garner, And Miguel Navascués
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2169 (2026).

Non-commutative polynomial optimization (NPO) problems seek to minimize the state average of a polynomial of some operator variables, subject to polynomial constraints, over all states and operators, as well as the Hilbert spaces where those might be defined. Many of these problems are known to admit a complete hierarchy of semidefinite programming (SDP) relaxations. In this work, we consider a variant of NPO problems where a subset of the operator variables satisfies a system of ordinary differential equations. We prove that, under mild conditions of operator boundedness, for every such problem one can construct a standard NPO problem with the same solution. This allows us to define a complete hierarchy of SDPs to tackle the original differential problem. We apply this method to bound averages of local observables in quantum spin systems subject to a Hamiltonian evolution (i.e., a quench). We find that, even in the thermodynamic limit of infinitely many sites, low levels of the hierarchy provide very good approximations for reasonably long evolution times.

.
tldr: This paper extends non-commutative polynomial optimization to problems with differential constraints, enabling SDP relaxations for quantum spin systems under Hamiltonian evolution.
motivation: Many quantum optimization problems involve time-dependent constraints, but standard NPO cannot handle differential equations. The authors aim to bridge this gap.
method: They prove that under boundedness conditions, a differential NPO problem can be transformed into a standard NPO problem, allowing a complete hierarchy of SDP relaxations.
result: The method is applied to bound local observables in quantum spin systems after a quench, showing good approximations even in the thermodynamic limit for moderate times.
conclusion: This work provides a new tool for analyzing quantum dynamics with optimization techniques, relevant to quantum information and many-body physics.

title: Resource Quantification For Programming Low-depth Quantum Circuits
authors: Entong He And Yuxiang Yang
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2166 (2026).

Noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices pave the way for implementing quantum algorithms that offer quantum advantages over their classical counterparts. Due to the intrinsic noise and decoherence in the physical system, NISQ machines are naturally modeled as large-scale, low-depth quantum circuits. In practice, executing such circuits requires sending program states that encode the relevant instructions to a programmable quantum computer, typically through a cloud service. Existing programming approaches designed for generic unitary transformations are computationally inefficient in the low-depth setting, and therefore remain unsatisfactory. As such, to realize NISQ algorithms, it is crucial to find an efficient way to program low-depth circuits as the number of qubits [MATH] increases. Here, we investigate the circuit complexity and the size of quantum memory, known as the program cost, required to program low-depth brickwork circuits. We establish a tight worst-case program cost of [MATH] for universally programming low-depth brickwork circuits in the large-[MATH] regime. Moreover, we analyze the trade-off between the cost of describing the layout of local gates and the cost of programming them to implement the target unitaries via the light-cone argument. Our findings suggest that faithful gate-wise programming is essentially optimal in the low-depth regime.

.
tldr: This paper establishes tight worst-case program cost for programming low-depth brickwork circuits, showing that faithful gate-wise programming is essentially optimal.
motivation: Existing programming approaches for generic unitary transformations are inefficient for low-depth circuits typical of NISQ devices, motivating the need for efficient programming methods.
method: The authors analyze circuit complexity and quantum memory size (program cost) required to program low-depth brickwork circuits, using light-cone arguments to trade off layout description cost and programming cost.
result: They prove a tight worst-case program cost of O(n) for universally programming low-depth brickwork circuits in the large-n regime, and show that faithful gate-wise programming is essentially optimal.
conclusion: The findings provide a resource-theoretic characterization of programming low-depth circuits, guiding efficient implementation of NISQ algorithms.

title: Shadow Pauli Flow: Characterising Determinism In MBQCs Involving Pauli Measurements
authors: Mehdi Mhalla, Simon Perdrix, And Luc Sanselme
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2163 (2026).

We introduce a new characterisation of determinism in Measurement-Based Quantum Computing (MBQC). The one-way model consists in performing local measurements over a large entangled state represented by a graph. The ability to perform an overall deterministic computation requires a correction strategy because of the non-determinism of each measurement. The existence of such a correction strategy depends on the underlying open graph, which is a description of the resource state together with the basis of the performed measurements. GFlow is a well-known graphical characterisation of robust determinism in MBQC when every measurement is performed in some specific planes of the Bloch sphere. While Pauli measurements are ubiquitous in MBQC, GFlow fails to be necessary for determinism when a measurement-based quantum computation involves Pauli measurements. Pauli Flow was designed as a generalisation of GFlow to handle MBQC with Pauli measurements, and guarantees robust determinism, however, it has been shown more recently that it fails to be a necessary condition. Our contribution is twofold. First, we demonstrate that Pauli flow is actually necessary for robust determinism in a weaker sense: given an open graph, i.e. a resource state, a deterministic computation can be driven iff it has a Pauli flow. However, the Pauli flows do not reflect all the possible correction strategies over a particular resource state, and properties like measurement order or computational depth are not necessarily reflected by a Pauli flow. Thus, to characterise determinism in full generality, we introduce a further extension called Shadow Pauli Flow that we prove necessary and sufficient for robust determinism: An MBQC is robustly deterministic if and only if its correction strategy is consistent with a Shadow Pauli flow. Furthermore, we show that Shadow Pauli flow can be computed in polynomial time.

.
tldr: Introduces Shadow Pauli Flow, a necessary and sufficient condition for robust determinism in measurement-based quantum computing with Pauli measurements.
motivation: Previous characterizations like GFlow and Pauli Flow were insufficient for MBQC with Pauli measurements; a complete characterization was needed.
method: Extends Pauli Flow to Shadow Pauli Flow, proving its necessity and sufficiency for robust determinism, and provides a polynomial-time algorithm to compute it.
result: Shadow Pauli Flow is both necessary and sufficient for robust determinism in MBQC with Pauli measurements, and can be computed in polynomial time.
conclusion: This work provides a complete graphical characterization of determinism in MBQC with Pauli measurements, enabling efficient verification of deterministic computations.

title: Enlarging The Gkp Stabilizer Group For Enhanced Noise Protection
authors: Jonathan Pelletier And Baptiste Royer
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2156 (2026).

Encoding a qubit in a larger Hilbert space of an oscillator is an efficient way to protect its quantum information against decoherence. Promising examples of such bosonic encodings are the Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) codes. In this work, we investigate how redefining the stabilizer group of the GKP codes to include all operations with trivial action on the code space can contribute to the search for an optimal implementation of a logical circuit when it is affected by noise. We find the generators of the Gaussian stabilizer group, allowing us to search for different physical implementations of a Clifford operation. We then propose an algorithm that finds the optimal implementation of a given logical Clifford circuit on GKP codes, such that the state is less affected by loss errors during the computation. Finally, we demonstrate numerically, with logical randomized benchmarking, that such a compiler can increase the lifetime of square-GKP qubits while running Clifford circuits, compared to a random walk compiler.

.
tldr: This paper enlarges the GKP stabilizer group to include all operations with trivial action on the code space, enabling optimal implementation of logical Clifford circuits with enhanced noise protection.
motivation: GKP codes are promising for protecting quantum information in oscillators, but finding optimal physical implementations of logical circuits under noise is challenging. The authors aim to improve noise protection by redefining the stabilizer group.
method: They find the generators of the Gaussian stabilizer group and propose an algorithm that searches for the optimal implementation of a given logical Clifford circuit on GKP codes, minimizing loss errors during computation.
result: Numerical simulations using logical randomized benchmarking show that the compiler increases the lifetime of square-GKP qubits while running Clifford circuits compared to a random walk compiler.
conclusion: Redefining the stabilizer group and optimizing circuit implementations can significantly enhance noise protection for GKP codes, advancing fault-tolerant quantum computation.

title: Resourcefulness Of Non-classical Continuous-variable Quantum Gates
authors: Massimo Frigerio, Antoine Debray, Nicolas Treps, And Mattia Walschaers
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2155 (2026).

In continuous-variable quantum computation, identifying key elements that enable a quantum computational advantage is a long-standing issue. Starting from the standard results on the necessity of Wigner negativity, we develop a comprehensive and versatile approach in which the techniques of [MATH]-ordered quasiprobabilities are exploited to provide rigorous statements on the simulability of photonic quantum circuits consisting of previously characterized gates and thereby identifying the contribution of each quantum gate to the potential achievement of quantum computational advantage. This is achieved by means of an analysis of the so-called transfer function, allowing us to highlight the resourcefulness of a gate set. As such this technique can be straightforwardly applied to current continuous-variables quantum circuits, while also constraining the tolerable amount of losses above which any potential quantum advantage can be ruled out. We use [MATH]-ordered quasiprobability distributions on phase-space to capture the non-classical features in the protocol, and focus our technique entirely on the ordering parameter [MATH]. This allows us to highlight the resourcefulness and robustness to loss of a universal set of unitary gates comprising three distinct Gaussian gates and any non-Gaussian unitary gate, providing important insight on the role of non-Gaussianity.

.
tldr: This paper develops a framework using s-ordered quasiprobabilities to quantify the non-classical resources of continuous-variable quantum gates, linking Wigner negativity to quantum computational advantage.
motivation: Identifying the key resources that enable quantum computational advantage in continuous-variable quantum computation is a long-standing challenge.
method: The authors use s-ordered quasiprobability distributions and the transfer function to analyze the resourcefulness of a universal gate set, including Gaussian and non-Gaussian gates, and assess robustness to loss.
result: They provide rigorous statements on simulability of photonic circuits and identify the contribution of each gate to quantum advantage, also constraining the tolerable loss threshold.
conclusion: The technique offers a versatile tool for characterizing non-classicality in continuous-variable quantum circuits and can be applied to current experimental setups.

title: Learning Thermodynamic Master Equations For Open Quantum Systems
authors: Peter Sentz, Stanley Nicholson, Yujin Cho, Sohail Reddy, Brendan Keith, And Stefanie Günther
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2151 (2026).

The characterization of Hamiltonians and other components of open quantum dynamical systems plays a crucial role in quantum computing and other applications. Scientific machine learning techniques have been applied to this problem in a variety of ways, including by modeling with deep neural networks. However, the majority of mathematical models describing open quantum systems are linear, and the natural nonlinearities in learnable models have not been incorporated using physical principles. We present a data-driven model for open quantum systems that includes learnable, thermodynamically consistent terms. The trained model is interpretable, as it directly estimates the system Hamiltonian and linear components of coupling to the environment. We validate the model on synthetic two and three-level data, as well as experimental two-level data collected from a quantum device at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory.

.
tldr: A data-driven model for open quantum systems that learns thermodynamically consistent terms, validated on synthetic and experimental data.
motivation: Characterizing Hamiltonians and environmental couplings in open quantum systems is crucial for quantum computing, but existing models often lack thermodynamic consistency.
method: The authors propose a learnable model that incorporates nonlinear, thermodynamically consistent terms, directly estimating the system Hamiltonian and linear coupling components from data.
result: The model is validated on synthetic two- and three-level systems and experimental two-level data from a quantum device, demonstrating interpretability and accuracy.
conclusion: The approach provides a physically principled, interpretable machine learning framework for modeling open quantum systems, with potential applications in quantum device characterization.

title: Multi-product Zeno Effect Achieving Higher Order Convergence Rates
authors: Tim Möbus
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2148 (2026).

The quantum Zeno effect is a fundamental mechanism for implementing the effective dynamics of projected Hamiltonian and Lindbladian systems. It approximates the target projected evolution by interleaving Hamiltonian or Lindblad dynamics with quantum operations associated with the desired subspace. In contrast to the related Trotter product formula, the best-known convergence rate of the quantum Zeno effect is typically limited to order [MATH]. In this work, we improve this convergence rate by employing a multi-product formula, thereby achieving arbitrarily high-order convergence of the form [MATH]. This yields an improved approximation scheme for Zeno-like expectation values via an efficient post-processing method. The approach combines a modified Chernoff lemma, an adapted Dunford-Segal approximation, holomorphic functional calculus, and Chebyshev interpolation. We illustrate the method with the bosonic cat code and also consider the broader class of systems governed by the Bang-Bang decoupling method.

.
tldr: This paper improves the convergence rate of the quantum Zeno effect to arbitrarily high order using multi-product formulas, with applications to projected dynamics and Bang-Bang decoupling.
motivation: The quantum Zeno effect is a fundamental mechanism for implementing effective dynamics, but its convergence rate is typically limited to first order. Achieving higher-order convergence can improve approximation schemes for quantum simulation and control.
method: The authors combine a modified Chernoff lemma, an adapted Dunford-Segal approximation, holomorphic functional calculus, and Chebyshev interpolation to construct a multi-product formula that yields higher-order convergence for the Zeno effect.
result: They demonstrate arbitrarily high-order convergence rates of the form O(Δt^k) for the quantum Zeno effect, and illustrate the method with the bosonic cat code and Bang-Bang decoupling.
conclusion: The multi-product Zeno effect provides a systematic way to achieve higher-order approximations of projected dynamics, with potential applications in quantum simulation and error suppression.

title: Active Quantum Reservoir Engineering: Using A Qubit To Manipulate Its Environment
authors: Marcelo Janovitch, Matteo Brunelli, And Patrick P. Potts
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2143 (2026).

Quantum reservoir engineering leverages dissipative processes to achieve desired behaviour, with applications ranging from entanglement generation to quantum error correction. Therein, a structured environment acts as an entropy sink for the system and no time-dependent control over the system is required. We develop a theoretical framework for active reservoir engineering, where time-dependent control over a quantum system is used to manipulate its environment. In this case, the system may act as an entropy sink for the environment. Our framework captures the dynamical interplay between system and environment, and provides an intuitive picture of how finite-size effects and system-environment correlations allow for manipulating the environment by repeated initialisation of the quantum system. We illustrate our results with two examples: a superconducting qubit coupled to an environment of two-level systems and a semiconducting quantum dot coupled to nuclear spins. In both scenarios, we find qualitative agreement with previous experimental results, illustrating how active control can unlock new functionalities in open quantum systems.

.
tldr: A theoretical framework for active reservoir engineering where time-dependent control over a quantum system manipulates its environment, with applications to open quantum systems.
motivation: Standard quantum reservoir engineering uses structured environments as entropy sinks without active control; this work explores the reverse scenario where the system actively manipulates its environment, enabling new functionalities.
method: The authors develop a theoretical framework capturing the dynamical interplay between system and environment, including finite-size effects and correlations, and illustrate it with two examples: a superconducting qubit coupled to two-level systems and a quantum dot coupled to nuclear spins.
result: The framework shows that repeated initialization of the quantum system can manipulate the environment, and qualitative agreement with previous experimental results is found in both example scenarios.
conclusion: Active control can unlock new functionalities in open quantum systems, providing a complementary approach to standard reservoir engineering.

title: Fast Quantum Measurement Tomography With Optimal Error Bounds
authors: Leonardo Zambrano, Sergi Ramos-Calderer, And Richard Kueng
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2162 (2026).

We present a two-step protocol for quantum measurement tomography that is light on classical co-processing cost and still achieves optimal sample complexity. Given measurement data from a known probe state ensemble, we first apply least-squares estimation to produce an unconstrained approximation of the POVM, and then project this estimate onto the set of valid quantum measurements. For a POVM with [MATH] outcomes acting on a [MATH]-dimensional system, we show that the protocol requires [MATH] samples to achieve error [MATH] in worst-case distance, and [MATH] samples in average-case distance. We further establish two matching sample complexity lower bounds of [MATH] and [MATH] for any non-adaptive, single-copy POVM tomography protocol. Hence, our projected least squares POVM tomography is sample-optimal in both the dimension and the number of outcomes for both distances. Our method admits an analytic form when using global or local 2-designs as probe ensembles and enables rigorous non-asymptotic error guarantees. Finally, we also complement our findings with empirical performance studies carried out on a noisy superconducting quantum computer with flux-tunable transmon qubits.

.
tldr: A sample-optimal protocol for quantum measurement tomography using projected least squares estimation.
motivation: Efficiently characterizing quantum measurements is crucial for quantum information processing, but existing tomography methods often require heavy classical post-processing or are not sample-optimal.
method: The protocol first applies least-squares estimation to measurement data from known probe states, then projects the estimate onto the set of valid POVMs. It uses global or local 2-designs as probe ensembles.
result: The protocol achieves optimal sample complexity in both worst-case and average-case distance, with matching lower bounds. It also provides rigorous non-asymptotic error guarantees.
conclusion: This work provides a practical, sample-optimal method for quantum measurement tomography with analytic forms and experimental validation on a superconducting quantum computer.

title: Exploring Imaginary Coordinates: Disparity In The Shape Of Quantum State Space In Even And Odd Dimensions
authors: Simon Morelli, Santiago Llorens, And Jens Siewert
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2153 (2026).

The state of a finite-dimensional quantum system is described by a density matrix that can be decomposed into a real diagonal, a real off-diagonal and and an imaginary off-diagonal part. The latter plays a peculiar role. While it is intuitively clear that some of the imaginary coordinates cannot have the same extension as their real counterparts the precise relation is not obvious. We give a complete characterization of the constraints in terms of tight inequalities for real and imaginary Bloch-type coordinates. Our description entails a three-dimensional Bloch ball-type model for the state space. We uncover a surprising qualitative difference for the state-space boundaries in even and odd dimensions.

.
tldr: This paper fully characterizes the constraints on real and imaginary Bloch coordinates for finite-dimensional quantum states, revealing a qualitative difference in state-space boundaries between even and odd dimensions.
motivation: Understanding the geometry of quantum state space is fundamental to quantum information theory, and the role of imaginary coordinates has been less explored.
method: The authors derive tight inequalities for real and imaginary Bloch-type coordinates, constructing a three-dimensional Bloch ball model for the state space.
result: They provide a complete characterization of constraints and uncover a surprising disparity in the shape of state-space boundaries for even versus odd dimensions.
conclusion: The work offers new insights into the structure of quantum state space, with potential implications for entanglement theory and quantum information processing.

title: On The Addressability Problem On Css Codes
authors: Jérôme Guyot And Samuel Jaques
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2145 (2026).

Recent discoveries in asymptotically good quantum codes have intensified research on their application in quantum computation and fault-tolerant operations. This study focuses on the addressability problem within CSS codes: we ask what circuits might implement logical gates on strict subsets of logical qubits. With some notion of fault-tolerance, we prove several impossibility results: for CSS codes with non-zero rate, one cannot address a logical [MATH], [MATH], [MATH], or [MATH] to any non-empty strict subset of logical qubits using a circuit made only from 1-local Clifford gates. Furthermore, we show that one cannot permute the logical qubits in a code purely by permuting the physical qubits, if the rate of the code is (asymptotically) greater than 1/3 and the distance is at least 3. We can show a similar no-go result for [MATH]s and [MATH]s between two such high-rate codes, albeit under a more restrictive assumption on the circuit, which we call "global" (though recent addressable CCZ gates use global circuits). This work pioneers the study of distance-preserving addressability in quantum codes, mainly by considering automorphisms of the code. This perspective offers new insights and potential directions for future research. We argue that studying this trade off between addressability and efficiency of the codes is essential to understand better how to do efficient quantum computation.

.
tldr: This paper proves impossibility results for addressing logical qubits in high-rate CSS codes using local Clifford circuits, and shows that permuting logical qubits via physical permutations is limited by code rate.
motivation: Recent advances in asymptotically good quantum codes raise the question of how to implement logical gates on subsets of logical qubits, which is crucial for fault-tolerant quantum computation.
method: The authors use automorphism theory of CSS codes and combinatorial arguments to derive no-go theorems for addressability of logical Pauli and Clifford operations, and for permutation of logical qubits via physical permutations.
result: For CSS codes with non-zero rate, one cannot address logical X, Z, H, or S gates to a strict subset of logical qubits using 1-local Clifford circuits. Also, permuting logical qubits by physical permutations is impossible if the rate exceeds 1/3 and distance is at least 3.
conclusion: The trade-off between addressability and code efficiency is fundamental, and this work provides new insights into the limitations of fault-tolerant operations on quantum codes.

title: Hierarchically Discriminating Haar-randomness In Quantum States From A Black-box Device
authors: Hao Wang And Adrián Pérez-Salinas Xavier Bonet-Monroig
abstract: The concept of randomness in quantum computing has been central to constructing benchmarking tools, cryptographic protocols, as well as a proof of beyond-classical computation. Discerning whether quantum states (or unitaries) are randomly distributed is a computational task that requires an enormous amount of quantum computational resources. This work addresses such a challenge by introducing a hierarchical discrimination algorithm to efficiently test if a set of states generated from a black-box quantum device with an unknown distribution is (in)compatible with a random distribution. To this end, we reduce the complexity of the problem by selecting an observable with known spectrum to study the statistical properties of its expectation values with respect to the quantum states from an unknown (black-box) quantum device. Concurrently, we use our first technical result, a connection between Haar-randomness and the Dirichlet distribution, to analytically compute Haar-random moments of the observable. Our Haar-random discriminator test is then simply to compare those statistical moments, such that if fails the test, it is enough to state that the quantum device does not output randomly distributed states. Else, we can not (yet) confirm that the states follow a Haar-random distribution. We further provide an extension to this algorithm by permutation- and unitary-equivalent randomization of the observable at increasing computational resources, which allows us to more accurately state whether is compatible with Haar-randomness. We envision the use of the discriminator test as a quantum device benchmark, by discriminating whether the states generated are incompatible with Haar-randomness.
tldr: This paper introduces a hierarchical algorithm to test whether quantum states from a black-box device are Haar-random, using statistical moments of observables.
motivation: Discerning Haar-randomness in quantum states is computationally hard but important for benchmarking and cryptographic protocols. The authors aim to reduce this complexity.
method: They select an observable with known spectrum, compute its expectation values over the unknown state distribution, and compare statistical moments to analytically derived Haar-random moments using a connection to the Dirichlet distribution. The algorithm can be extended with randomized observables.
result: The test can efficiently rule out Haar-randomness if moments mismatch, but cannot confirm randomness; it provides a hierarchical discrimination with increasing computational resources.
conclusion: The discriminator test serves as a practical benchmark for quantum devices, identifying non-random state distributions with limited resources.

title: Optimal Schedule Of Multi-channel Quantum Zeno Dragging With Application To Solving The k-SAT Problem
authors: Yipei Zhang, Alain Sarlette, Philippe Lewalle, Tathagata Karmakar, Thilo Scharnhorst, And K. Birgitta Whaley
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2167 (2026).

Quantum Zeno dragging enables the preparation of common eigenstates of a set of observables by frequent measurement and adiabatic-like modulation of the measurement basis. In this work, we present a deeper analysis of multi-channel Zeno dragging using generalized measurements, i.e. simultaneously measuring a set of non-commuting observables that vary slowly in time, to drag the state towards a target subspace. For concreteness, we will focus on a measurement-driven approach to solving k-SAT problems as examples. We first compute some analytical upper bounds on the convergence time, including the effect of finite measurement time resolution. We then apply optimal control theory to obtain the optimal dragging schedule that lower bounds the convergence time, for low-dimensional settings. This study provides a theoretical foundation for multi-channel Zeno dragging and its optimization, and also serves as a guide for designing optimal dragging schedules for quantum information tasks including measurement-driven quantum algorithms.

.
tldr: This paper analyzes multi-channel quantum Zeno dragging with generalized measurements and applies optimal control to schedule measurements for solving k-SAT problems.
motivation: Quantum Zeno dragging can prepare common eigenstates of observables, which is useful for measurement-driven quantum algorithms like solving k-SAT. The authors aim to optimize the dragging schedule to minimize convergence time.
method: The authors derive analytical upper bounds on convergence time, including finite measurement resolution effects, and apply optimal control theory to find the optimal dragging schedule in low-dimensional settings.
result: They obtain lower bounds on convergence time and demonstrate the optimal schedule for multi-channel Zeno dragging, providing a theoretical foundation for measurement-driven quantum algorithms.
conclusion: The work offers a guide for designing optimal dragging schedules for quantum information tasks, particularly measurement-driven quantum algorithms.

title: Steady-state Entanglement Harvesting For Two Rotating Atoms In A Cylindrical Cavity
authors: Hong-Tao Zheng, Xiang-Fa Zhou, Guang-Can Guo And Zheng-Wei Zhou
abstract: We study the entanglement dynamics of two rotating atoms (with two internal levels and ) in a cylindrical cavity, which interact with a massless scalar field in vacuum satisfying the Dirichlet boundary condition. Our analysis demonstrates that it is possible to obtain the steady-state entanglement under two types of resonant conditions. For two identical atoms with the same world-line, the system reduces to the usual dissipative Dicke model at the first resonant condition where and are the energy splitting and the angular velocity of the th atom, and is the Lorentz factor. The entangled steady-state takes the form where and are constant, which is consistent with the previous study (see 2022 Phys. Rev. D 106 105028). For two atoms with different world-lines, the system suffers from a significant mixed joint dissipation process at the second resonant condition , and reaches an entangled steady-state as . Moreover, with the help of the cavity, we can obtain a much higher concurrence in the final states by changing the relative ratio of the two orbital radii. Our work thus provides a more effective way for the extraction of steady-state entanglement from the vacuum via the analogue Unruh effect for two rotating atoms in a cylindrical cavity.
tldr: Two rotating atoms in a cylindrical cavity can harvest steady-state entanglement from the vacuum via the analogue Unruh effect, with cavity geometry enhancing concurrence.
motivation: To explore steady-state entanglement harvesting from vacuum using rotating atoms, which is relevant to quantum thermodynamics and information extraction.
method: The authors model two two-level atoms rotating in a cylindrical cavity with Dirichlet boundary conditions, interacting with a massless scalar field. They solve the master equation under two resonant conditions and compute concurrence.
result: Steady-state entanglement is achieved under two resonant conditions; for identical atoms it reduces to the Dicke model, while for different world-lines a mixed dissipation process occurs. Cavity geometry allows higher concurrence by tuning orbital radii.
conclusion: The work provides an effective method for extracting steady-state entanglement from vacuum using rotating atoms in a cavity, with potential applications in quantum information processing.

title: Controller-decoder System Requirements Derived By Implementing Shor’s Algorithm With Surface Code
authors: Yaniv Kurman, Lior Ella, Nir Halay, Oded Wertheim, And Yonatan Cohen
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2170 (2026).

Quantum Error Correction (QEC) is regarded as the most promising path to quantum advantage. The success of QEC relies on achieving quantum gate fidelities below the error threshold of the QEC code, while accurately decoding errors through classical processing of the QEC stabilizer measurements. In this paper, we uncover the critical system-level requirements from a controller-decoder system (CDS) necessary to successfully execute the next milestone in QEC: a non-Clifford circuit. Using a representative non-Clifford circuit, of Shor factorization algorithm for the number 21, we convert the logical-level circuit to a QEC surface code circuit and finally to the physical level circuit. By taking into account realistic implementation aspects using typical superconducting qubit processor parameters, we reveal a broad range of core requirements from any CDS aimed at performing error corrected quantum computation. Our findings indicate that the controller-decoder closed-loop latency must remain within tens of microseconds, achievable by distributing decoding data into several decoders while ensuring fast communication between decoders and with the controller. By extending existing simulation techniques, we simulate the complete fault-tolerant factorization circuit at the physical level, demonstrating that near-term hardware performance in the scale of 0.1% physical error rates and 1000 qubits, are sufficient for a successful circuit execution. Overall, the requirements outlined here set the stage for near- and medium-term experimental realizations of non-Clifford QEC circuits.

A video of the physical-level gate sequences for the factorization circuit with distance-3 surfaces. (doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.17970554)

.
tldr: This paper derives system-level requirements for a controller-decoder system to execute Shor's algorithm with surface code error correction, using realistic superconducting qubit parameters.
motivation: Executing non-Clifford circuits with quantum error correction is a key milestone, but system-level requirements for the controller-decoder system are not well understood.
method: The authors convert a logical Shor's algorithm circuit for factoring 21 into a surface code circuit and then to physical-level operations, simulating the complete fault-tolerant circuit with realistic hardware parameters.
result: They find that controller-decoder closed-loop latency must be within tens of microseconds, achievable by distributing decoding data, and that near-term hardware with 0.1% error rates and 1000 qubits suffices for successful execution.
conclusion: The outlined requirements set the stage for near- and medium-term experimental realizations of non-Clifford QEC circuits.

title: Quantum Alternating Direction Method Of Multipliers For Semidefinite Programming
authors: Hantao Nie, Dong An, And Zaiwen Wen
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2154 (2026).

Semidefinite programming (SDP) is a fundamental convex optimization problem with wide-ranging applications. However, solving large-scale instances remains computationally challenging due to the high cost of solving linear systems and performing eigenvalue decompositions. In this paper, we present a quantum alternating direction method of multipliers (QADMM) for SDPs, building on recent advances in quantum computing. An inexact ADMM framework is developed, which tolerates errors in the iterates arising from block-encoding approximation and quantum measurement. Within this robust scheme, we design a polynomial proximal operator to address the semidefinite conic constraints and apply the quantum singular value transformation to accelerate the most costly projection updates. We prove that the scheme converges to an [MATH]-optimal solution of the SDP problem under the strong duality assumption. A detailed complexity analysis shows that the QADMM algorithm achieves favorable scaling with respect to dimension compared to the classical ADMM algorithm and quantum interior point methods, highlighting its potential for solving large-scale SDPs.

.
tldr: Proposes a quantum algorithm for semidefinite programming using ADMM and quantum singular value transformation.
motivation: Solving large-scale SDPs is computationally expensive; quantum computing may offer speedups.
method: Develops an inexact ADMM framework that tolerates errors from block-encoding and measurement, and uses quantum singular value transformation for projection updates.
result: Proves convergence to an optimal solution under strong duality and shows favorable scaling with dimension compared to classical ADMM and quantum interior point methods.
conclusion: QADMM is a promising quantum algorithm for large-scale SDPs, though practical implementation remains challenging.

title: Query And Depth Upper Bounds For Quantum Unitaries Via Grover Search
authors: Gregory Rosenthal
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2144 (2026).

We prove that any [MATH]-qubit unitary can be implemented (i) approximately in time [MATH] with query access to an appropriate classical oracle, and also (ii) exactly by a circuit of depth [MATH] with one- and two-qubit gates and [MATH] ancillae. The proofs involve similar reductions to Grover search. The proof of (ii) also involves a linear-depth construction of arbitrary quantum states using one- and two-qubit gates (in fact, this can be improved to constant depth with the addition of fanout and generalized Toffoli gates) which may be of independent interest. We also prove a matching [MATH] lower bound for (i) and (ii) for a certain class of implementations.

.
tldr: This paper proves upper bounds on query complexity and circuit depth for implementing arbitrary quantum unitaries using Grover search, with matching lower bounds for certain implementations.
motivation: Understanding the resources required to implement arbitrary quantum operations is fundamental to quantum computing. The paper aims to establish tight bounds on query complexity and circuit depth for unitary synthesis.
method: The authors reduce unitary implementation to Grover search, showing that any n-qubit unitary can be approximated or exactly implemented with O(2^{n/2}) queries or depth, using a linear-depth construction for arbitrary quantum states.
result: Upper bounds of O(2^{n/2}) for both approximate query complexity and exact circuit depth are proven, along with a matching Ω(2^{n/2}) lower bound for a class of implementations.
conclusion: The results provide nearly optimal resource estimates for unitary synthesis, highlighting the power of Grover search in this context.

title: Searching For Quantum Effects In The Brain: A Bell-type Test For Nonclassical Latent Representations In Autoencoders
authors: Iannis K Kominis, Can Xie, Shuguang Li, Michael Skotiniotis And Giorgos P Tsironis
abstract: Whether neural information processing is entirely classical or involves quantum-mechanical elements remains an open question. Here we propose a model-agnostic, information-theoretic test of nonclassicality that bypasses microscopic assumptions and instead probes the structure of neural representations themselves. Using autoencoders as a transparent model system, we introduce a Bell-type consistency test in latent space, and ask whether decoding statistics obtained under multiple readout contexts can be jointly explained by a single positive latent-variable distribution. By shifting the search for quantum-like signatures in neural systems from microscopic dynamics to experimentally testable constraints on information processing, this work opens a new route for probing the fundamental physics of neural computation. The proposed test identifies violations of classical latent-variable consistency at the level of statistical representations, without assuming a specific underlying physical mechanism.
tldr: Proposes a Bell-type consistency test for nonclassical latent representations in autoencoders, searching for quantum-like signatures in neural information processing.
motivation: Whether neural computation involves quantum effects remains unknown; the paper aims to bypass microscopic assumptions and test nonclassicality at the level of statistical representations.
method: Uses autoencoders as a model system and introduces a Bell-type test in latent space, checking whether decoding statistics under multiple readout contexts can be explained by a single classical latent-variable distribution.
result: The test identifies violations of classical latent-variable consistency, indicating potential nonclassical signatures in neural representations.
conclusion: This work opens a new route for probing quantum-like effects in neural systems through information-theoretic constraints, without assuming a specific physical mechanism.

title: Invariant Nonequilibrium Dynamics In Gene Regulation Optimize Information Flow
authors: Benjamin Zolleralexis Bénichouthomas Gregorgašper Tkačikahttps://ror.org/0495fxg12department Of Stem Cell And Developmental Biology, CNRS UMR3738 Paris Cité, Institut Pasteur, Paris Fr-75015, Francebhttps://ror.org/03gnh5541institute Of Science And Technology Austria, Klosterneuburg At-3400, Austriachttps://ror.org/00hx57361joseph Henry Laboratories Of Physics, Lewis-Sigler Institute For Integrative Genomics, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ 08544
abstract:
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, Volume 123, Issue 28, July 2026.
SignificanceEukaryotic genes switch on and off stochastically, yet cells regulate gene expression with remarkable precision by biasing the probability of switching. Recent experiments revealed a surprising and unexplained constraint: The characteristic ...
tldr: This paper studies nonequilibrium dynamics in gene regulation and shows that invariant dynamics optimize information flow, linking thermodynamics to biological information processing.
motivation: Recent experiments revealed a surprising constraint in eukaryotic gene regulation: the characteristic timescales of activation and inactivation are invariant across different conditions. The authors aim to understand why this invariance exists and its functional role.
method: The authors develop a theoretical model of stochastic gene expression as a nonequilibrium process, using information theory and thermodynamics to analyze the trade-off between speed, accuracy, and energy dissipation. They derive bounds on information flow and show that invariant dynamics achieve optimal information transmission.
result: They find that the observed invariant dynamics maximize the mutual information between input signals and gene expression levels, given constraints on energy dissipation and response time. This provides a thermodynamic explanation for the experimental observations.
conclusion: The work demonstrates that nonequilibrium dynamics in gene regulation are optimized for information flow, bridging thermodynamics and information theory in a biological context.

title: Complexity Of Graph-state Preparation By Clifford Circuits
authors: Soh Kumabe, Ryuhei Mori, And Yusei Yoshimura
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2165 (2026).

In this work, we study the complexity of graph-state preparation in a general model of quantum algorithms that allows measurements in the computational basis, single-qubit Clifford operations, and two-qubit Clifford operations. We define the CZ-complexity of a graph state [MATH] as the minimum number of two-qubit Clifford operations required to generate [MATH] from [MATH] for some [MATH]. Equivalently, every optimal algorithm can be taken to use only controlled-Z (CZ) gates as its two-qubit Clifford operations. We then give a combinatorial characterization of graph-state transformations. Specifically, [MATH] can be generated from another graph state [MATH] by an algorithm of CZ-complexity at most [MATH] if and only if [MATH] can be obtained from [MATH] by vertex deletions, local complementations and at most [MATH] elementary edge-complementations. Here, an elementary edge-complementation toggles either a single edge, all edges between one vertex and the neighborhood of another, or all edges between the neighborhoods of two non-adjacent vertices. Using this characterization, we relate CZ-complexity to rank-width. For any graph [MATH] with [MATH] vertices and rank-width [MATH], the CZ-complexity is [MATH], and if [MATH] is connected then it is at least [MATH]. We also show that these bounds are close to optimal. Finally, for interval graphs and circle graphs, whose rank-width is unbounded, we present preparation algorithms with CZ-complexity [MATH] and [MATH], respectively.

.
tldr: This paper studies the minimum number of two-qubit Clifford operations (CZ-complexity) needed to prepare graph states, providing a combinatorial characterization and bounds based on rank-width.
motivation: Understanding the complexity of graph-state preparation is important for quantum computing and networking, but the paper focuses on circuit complexity rather than information-theoretic or thermodynamic aspects.
method: The authors define CZ-complexity and characterize graph-state transformations using vertex deletions, local complementations, and elementary edge-complementations. They relate CZ-complexity to rank-width and provide algorithms for interval and circle graphs.
result: For any graph with n vertices and rank-width r, the CZ-complexity is O(n log n) and at least Ω(r) for connected graphs. Interval and circle graphs have O(n) and O(n log n) CZ-complexity, respectively.
conclusion: The paper provides a combinatorial understanding of graph-state preparation complexity, but it is more aligned with quantum circuit complexity and graph theory than with the core interests in quantum information theory or thermodynamics.

title: Exact Quantum Many-Body Scars In 2d Quantum Gauge Models
authors: Yuan Miao, Linhao Li, Hosho Katsura, And Masahito Yamazaki
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2164 (2026).

Quantum many-body scars (QMBS) serve as important examples of ergodicity-breaking phenomena in quantum many-body systems. Despite recent extensive studies, exact QMBS are rare in dimensions higher than one. In this paper, we study a two-dimensional quantum [MATH] gauge model that is dual to a two-dimensional spin-[MATH] XY model defined on bipartite graphs. We identify the exact eigenstates of the XY model with a tower structure as exact QMBS. Exploiting the duality transformation, we show that the exact QMBS of the XY model (and XXZ model) after the transformation are the exact QMBS of the dual [MATH] gauge model. This construction is versatile and has potential applications for finding new QMBS in other higher-dimensional models.

.
tldr: This paper constructs exact quantum many-body scars in a 2D quantum gauge model via duality to an XY model.
motivation: Quantum many-body scars are rare in higher dimensions; the authors aim to provide exact examples in 2D.
method: They study a 2D quantum Z2 gauge model dual to a spin-1/2 XY model on bipartite graphs, identifying exact eigenstates with a tower structure as scars.
result: Exact QMBS are found in the XY model and, via duality, in the gauge model, demonstrating a versatile construction.
conclusion: This work provides new exact QMBS in 2D, with potential for extension to other higher-dimensional models.

title: Machine Learning Decoding Of Circuit-Level Noise For Bivariate Bicycle Codes
authors: John Blue, Harshil Avlani, Zhiyang He, Liu Ziyin, And Isaac L. Chuang
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2149 (2026).

Fault-tolerant quantum computers will depend crucially on the performance of the classical decoding algorithm which takes in the results of measurements and outputs corrections to the errors inferred to have occurred. Machine learning models have shown great promise as decoders for the surface code; however, this promise has not yet been substantiated for the more challenging task of decoding quantum low-density parity-check (QLDPC) codes. In this paper, we present a recurrent, transformer-based neural network designed to decode circuit-level noise on Bivariate Bicycle (BB) codes. For the [MATH] BB code, at a physical error rate of [MATH], our model achieves logical error rates almost [MATH] times lower than belief propagation with ordered statistics decoding (BP-OSD), and roughly [MATH] times larger than a most-likely error decoder. Moreover, while BP-OSD has a wide distribution of runtimes with significant outliers, our model has a consistent runtime and is an order-of-magnitude faster than the worst-case times from a benchmark BP-OSD implementation. On the [MATH] BB code, our model obtains worse logical error rates but maintains the speed advantage. These results provide initial evidence that machine learning decoders can out-perform conventional decoders on small QLDPC codes, but suggest more complex architectures and/or training procedures are necessary to scale to larger code sizes.

.
tldr: This paper applies machine learning decoding to bivariate bicycle codes, a type of QLDPC code, achieving lower logical error rates and faster runtime than BP-OSD on small codes.
motivation: Fault-tolerant quantum computers require efficient decoders, and machine learning decoders have shown promise for surface codes but not yet for QLDPC codes, which are more challenging.
method: A recurrent, transformer-based neural network is designed to decode circuit-level noise on bivariate bicycle codes, trained on simulated error data.
result: On the [[144,12,12]] BB code, the ML decoder achieves logical error rates almost 10 times lower than BP-OSD and is an order of magnitude faster, but on the [[288,12,18]] code it performs worse while maintaining speed advantage.
conclusion: Machine learning decoders can outperform conventional decoders on small QLDPC codes, but scaling to larger codes requires more complex architectures or training procedures.

title: High-gain Effects In Broadband Continuous-wave Parametric Down Conversion Sources And Measurements With Undetected Photons
authors: Martin Houde, Franz Roeder, Christine Silberhorn, Benjamin Brecht And Nicolás Quesada
abstract: We study theoretically how high-gain effects affect the measurement outcome of visible signal spectra in undetected photon measurement schemes. We consider two interferometric configurations: firstly, the SU(1,1) interferometer where the idler incurs loss and additional dispersion in between two identical, lossless, squeezers; secondly, the induced coherence interferometer where the idler incurs loss and additional dispersion in between two identical, lossless, squeezers and where the second squeezer is seeded by the idler and a vacuum ancilla mode. Furthermore, we consider a distributed loss configuration where the idler incurs loss as it propagates in the nonlinear medium. Motivated by experimental evidence and due to the fact that broadband sources are ideal for these measurement schemes, we use the dispersive data of a third-order dispersion engineered integrated waveguide parametric down conversion (PDC) source presented in Roeder et al (2024 New J. Phys. 26 123025) to model the PDC spectra in the three configurations. For each configuration we consider the case of idler-only (i) absorption, (ii) additional dispersion, and (iii) the combined effects. We obtain results which outline the strength and weaknesses of the different configurations at different operation points.
tldr: The paper theoretically studies high-gain effects in broadband continuous-wave parametric down conversion sources for measurements with undetected photons, focusing on interferometric configurations.
motivation: Understanding high-gain effects is important for improving the performance of quantum measurement schemes that rely on undetected photons, which are relevant to quantum imaging and sensing.
method: The authors model parametric down conversion spectra in SU(1,1) and induced coherence interferometers, considering idler loss and dispersion, using dispersive data from an integrated waveguide source.
result: They outline the strengths and weaknesses of different configurations at various operation points, showing how high-gain affects measurement outcomes.
conclusion: The study provides insights into optimizing broadband PDC sources for undetected photon measurements, but the work is primarily about source characterization and interferometry rather than quantum networking.

title: Cavity-induced Multispin Interactions And Phase Transitions In Ultracold Fermi Gases
authors: Shi-Liang Zhu And Z D Wang Zhen Zheng
abstract: The many-body physics of higher-spin systems is expected to host qualitatively new matter phases, but realizing them requires the controllable interactions between multispin components that can be tuned independently for each component. Here we propose a scheme that meets this demand in ultracold Fermi gases. By engineering the atom-cavity coupling, we generate cavity-induced effective interactions between pseudo-spin states via multiple Raman and cavity paths. Focusing on the simplest spin-1 case, we obtain two independent scattering channels whose relative strengths and signs are determined by the Clebsch–Gordan coefficients and optical-field parameters. The resulting Hamiltonian combines the on-site Cooper pairing with the off-site repulsion, and drives a continuous transition from the superfluid to the spin-density-wave phase. The coexistence region is reminiscent of a supersolid, yet the self-organized modulation appears in the spin density profile of a higher-spin representation, rather than in the number density profile. The proposal can be implemented with the existing techniques in ultracold atoms. Therefore it offers a versatile platform for quantum simulation of higher-spin many-body physics.
tldr: This paper proposes a scheme to realize cavity-induced multispin interactions in ultracold Fermi gases, leading to a superfluid to spin-density-wave phase transition.
motivation: Higher-spin systems can host new quantum phases, but controllable multispin interactions are challenging to achieve.
method: By engineering atom-cavity coupling via multiple Raman and cavity paths, effective interactions between pseudo-spin states are generated, with independent control over scattering channels.
result: The resulting Hamiltonian drives a continuous transition from superfluid to spin-density-wave phase, with a coexistence region reminiscent of supersolid but in spin density.
conclusion: The scheme offers a versatile platform for quantum simulation of higher-spin many-body physics using existing ultracold atom techniques.

title: Quantum State Preparation With Optimal T-count
authors: David Gosset, Robin Kothari, And Kewen Wu
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2168 (2026).

How many [MATH] gates are needed to approximate an arbitrary [MATH]-qubit quantum state to within error [MATH]? Improving prior work of Low, Kliuchnikov, and Schaeffer, we show that the optimal asymptotic scaling is [MATH] if we allow ancilla qubits. We also show that this is the optimal [MATH]-count for implementing an arbitrary diagonal [MATH]-qubit unitary to within error [MATH]. We describe applications in which a tensor product of many single-qubit unitaries can be synthesized in parallel for the price of one.

.
